courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice
md: 3DGS trades memory for speed: hundreds of megabytes of explicit parameters instead of a few megabytes of network weights, in exchange for rendering at well over 30 FPS and training in tens of minutes.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Add-one-in vs leave-one-out on a fixed harness
md: Removing a stage is not always a clean subtraction. You must decide what replaces it: no rewrite at all, or a trivial rewrite; BM25 alone, or BM25 with more candidates to keep the reranker's input size equal. State the replacement, because different choices give different deltas.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: SWE-bench: how one patch gets graded
md: Resolved means: the patch applies, and **every** FAIL_TO_PASS test and **every** PASS_TO_PASS test is found and passes. Fixing the issue while breaking one old test scores exactly the same as doing nothing.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Designing tools: the agent-computer interface
md: Treat tool design like UI design for a new colleague: clear names, documented parameters, concise high-signal output, guardrails that turn likely mistakes into instructive errors. Changing the tool often beats changing the prompt.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
md: Verification turns "the agent says it is done" into "independent evidence says it is done". How much you can trust a shipped result is bounded by how often the verifier passes wrong results.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Reward design: hidden tests, partial credit and judges
md: Partial credit is not automatically better. A reward that counts tests which already passed pays the agent for the starting state, so on hard tasks the policy can learn that touching nothing beats trying. Credit only the change you want, and make breaking existing behavior cost something.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Why AI text needs a planted signal
md: The hard rule damages **low-entropy** text, where one continuation is nearly forced. The paper's example: "Barack" is almost always followed by "Obama", yet "Obama" may be on the red list. Code and memorized text have the same problem. The next lesson fixes this with a soft bias.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: What an allocation trace records and why you would replay it
md: Live bytes are not RSS. RSS counts whole pages the process has touched, including allocator metadata, rounding and free holes. The gap between the two is the overhead you are usually hunting.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Local Outlier Factor: density compared with your neighbors
md: scikit-learn's LocalOutlierFactor has two modes. With novelty=False (the default) only fit_predict and negative_outlier_factor_ exist. With novelty=True you get predict, decision_function and score_samples, but the docs warn to call them only on new data: scoring the training points that way gives wrong results, and predict will not match fit_predict.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Commit, abort with CLRs, and fuzzy checkpoints
md: A checkpoint is not a point where the disk is consistent. A fuzzy checkpoint only records which transactions were active and which pages were dirty. Redo usually has to start **before** the checkpoint, at the smallest recLSN in the DPT, because a page dirtied long ago may still be unflushed.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Input-type bugs in real pipelines
md: Record the model id and the input type (or exact prefix string) alongside the index, and check them at query time. When either changes, build a new index and switch over, rather than re-embedding part of the old one in place.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Why waiting on threads is expensive and coroutines are cheap
md: Async does not make one request faster. It makes **waiting cheap**: a waiting connection costs a small saved object instead of a blocked OS thread with its own stack, so a few threads can serve many thousands of mostly idle connections.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS compares values, not history. If the value goes from A to B and back to A between your load and your CAS, the CAS succeeds as if nothing happened. For a counter that is harmless. For pointers in lock-free data structures it can be a real bug, the **ABA problem**, which has its own course later.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Why research needs a loop, not one retrieval
md: A research agent is not a bigger retrieval call. It is a harness loop whose next query depends on what the last read revealed, and whose output is a set of claims each tied to a source.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions
md: "Matmul becomes additions" applies to the weight matrices. Attention scores (Q times K, then weights times V) multiply activations by activations, so they are not ternary. And the speedup only appears with a kernel that actually exploits ternary weights, which lesson 5 covers.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Global history, gshare, TAGE and perceptron predictors
md: A perceptron can only learn *linearly separable* functions of history. A branch that is taken when exactly one of two earlier branches was taken (an XOR) cannot be learned perfectly, while a table of counters indexed by history can learn any function given enough entries. That is why the paper also evaluated a gshare plus perceptron hybrid.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
md: Bloom filters only help point lookups. A range scan must open every run that overlaps the range and merge them, so the RocksDB guide counts scan read amplification as (L0 files) + (non-empty levels). Tiered layouts with many runs pay most for scans.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: 2Q, InnoDB midpoint insertion and PostgreSQL ring buffers
md: Real systems combine a cheap recency approximation with a second signal: PostgreSQL uses counts plus per-operation rings, InnoDB uses a two-segment list with a time threshold, and 2Q and LRU-2 use a remembered first reference. The common goal: a page must prove reuse before it can displace the hot set.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit
md: Byte models trade a tokenizer for an extra design choice: how to group bytes. With learned, entropy-based patches, BLT matched BPE models at 8B for equal training FLOPs, improved robustness and spelling, and turned patch size into a knob that trades steps for model size.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Why one load can cost 3 cycles or 240
md: You never call the cache. The only levers you have are **which addresses you touch and in what order**: data layout and access pattern. That is what the rest of this course makes precise.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Why tracing circuits needs a replacement model
md: Attribution graphs trade the real model for an interpretable stand-in whose direct interactions are linear on one prompt. Every claim read off the graph is a hypothesis about the real model until an intervention confirms it.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: Only clicked documents need propensities, and the estimate is unbiased only if the propensities are correct and every relevant document has a nonzero chance of being observed. Joachims et al. also require that propensities depend only on logged information (unconfoundedness).

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with prompts, probes and robustness
md: Robustness does not survive adapting CLIP to ImageNet. Fitting a logistic-regression classifier on CLIP features with ImageNet labels raised ImageNet accuracy by 9.2% to 85.4%, yet average accuracy across the shifted datasets slightly decreased. Gains on the training distribution and robustness are different things.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Why analytic scans want columns, not rows
md: Columns win when queries read few columns of many rows; rows win for point reads and frequent updates of whole records. The layout decides how many bytes a scan must move.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: What -O0, -O2 and -O3 actually switch on
md: An -O level is a bundle of passes. -O0 keeps every variable in memory for debuggability; -O2 is the standard speed level; -O3, -Os, -Og and -Ofast each trade something (size, speed, debuggability, strictness) for something else.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
md: PGO, -march and fast-math can each beat any -O level, but each adds a condition: representative profiles, a known target CPU, and numerics that tolerate reordering.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
md: A concurrent test that passes tells you only that the schedules your machine happened to pick were fine. To learn anything about the others you must either enumerate schedules (loom) or check the ordering rules on the schedule you got (TSan).

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Why one big ODE step from noise collapses to the mean
md: A diffusion model knows the *local* direction at each point. One-step generation needs the *global* answer: where does the whole trajectory end? A consistency model learns that endpoint directly.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Why quorum overlap alone is not linearizable, and the fix
md: W + R > N guarantees that a read sees every *completed* write. Linearizability also needs reads to agree with each other while a write is in flight. ABD gets that by making each read finish only after its result sits on a quorum.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Consistent hashing with bounded loads: a hard cap per server
md: The balance factor c is a dial between two goods: low c gives tight balance but forwards more requests away from their natural owner (more misses for caches); high c keeps affinity but tolerates more imbalance.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
md: Arc consistency is not the same as a solution. Three variables with domain $\{1,2\}$ and pairwise $\neq$ constraints are fully arc-consistent (every value has a support on every arc), yet no assignment satisfies all three. Propagation shrinks the search; it does not replace it.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Deletes and resets are rare in training data and rare in casual testing, so they are the operations most likely to be broken in your system. Test them on purpose: write cases for *drop X*, *any X is fine*, *never mind the Y* and *start over*.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Storing state server-side and measuring it
md: Store the state server-side with a version and an event log; evaluate it with joint goal accuracy and per-operation recall, not just slot accuracy or end-to-end clicks.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: The naive loop: four stages, one at a time
md: The naive loop is slow for a scheduling reason, not a kernel reason. Three units that could run at once are being used one at a time. The rest of this course is the machinery for filling those holes: **pinned memory** (so copies can be asynchronous), **streams** (so work can be queued independently), **events** (so order is expressed without stalling), and **graphs** (so launching the work is cheap).

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: From [CLS] to a score: logits, sigmoid and monoT5's true token
md: Sigmoid is monotonic, so it never changes the order of candidates. The Sentence Transformers docs say so explicitly: MS MARCO models return logits, and adding a Sigmoid activation gives 0 to 1 scores without changing the ranking. Use sigmoid when you need a threshold or a comparable confidence, not to improve ranking.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
md: Atoms are hardware facts, TiledMMA and TiledCopy are spatial arrangements of atoms, and partition_A/B/C or partition_S/D turn a tile into per-thread fragments. Swapping the atom (FMA, mma.sync, wgmma) changes the instruction without rewriting the loops.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: CXL protocols, device types and the path of one load
md: Pooling and sharing are different. In **pooling** each slice of memory belongs to exactly one host at a time; it just moves between hosts. In **sharing** (CXL 3.0) several hosts map the same bytes at once and hardware keeps them coherent. Most CXL disaggregation designs, including Pond, use pooling.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The 3-step pipeline and what it did to The Pile
md: The toy curves are the paper's closed-form error formula, $(n H + s^2 \Delta)/(n+s)^2$ with $s = 1$, for unigram models. Here $H = \sum_x p(x)(1-p(x))$ is the paper's difficulty term (not Shannon entropy) and $\Delta$ is the squared distance of the uniform prior from the truth. Real LMs are not unigram estimators; the toy shows that a no-tradeoff reweighting is possible, not that it always exists.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
md: Vectorizing the instructions does not fix the layout. Even if a compiler vectorizes an AoS loop, the x values are still 12 bytes apart, so each register still needs a gather and the loop still pays for every unused byte in each line.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time
md: Determinism leaks are easy to write. Reading the real clock, spawning an OS thread, seeding from OS entropy, or iterating a hash map whose order is randomized per process (Rust's default `HashMap` is) all make the same seed produce different runs. FoundationDB avoids multithreaded concurrency entirely and deploys one node per core instead.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Sampling: predict every mask, keep the confident, remask the rest
md: A sampling step is: one forward pass over the whole sequence, a guess at every masked slot, then keep the k most confident guesses and remask the rest. The schedule fixes k per step; the confidence ranking decides the order.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Moving the KV cache: bytes, links and overlap
md: Transfer cost = prompt tokens x bytes per token / bandwidth. Grouped-query attention, layer-wise streaming and placement on fast links make it small; slow links and long prompts at high rates make it the bottleneck.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO swaps variables: instead of learning a reward and then the policy it implies, it learns the policy directly and reads the reward off it as $\hat r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$. This is the paper's subtitle: your language model is secretly a reward model.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Until phase 4, at least one store is complete and current, and the other one is being kept in step with it. That is what makes every earlier step reversible. Plan each phase so it can be rolled out gradually (by percentage of objects or code paths) and rolled back with a flag.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path
md: Move one thing at a time, keep one store complete until the very end, and measure agreement continuously. The deletion in phase 4 is the only step that should be hard to undo.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Affine quantization: storing reals as int8 plus a scale
md: Misconception: int8 means the model can only represent values between -128 and 127. The integers are codes; the scale maps them to any real range. What int8 limits is the number of distinct levels (256) inside that range, so the range you pick matters more than the bit width alone.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt
md: Length control needs an online reward that sees the generated length. The prompt carries the budget; the RL reward is what teaches the model to honor it.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Scoring a disaggregation: MAE, NEP, NDE and F1
md: Metric details change numbers silently. The on/off threshold (10 W in NILMTK) sets F1; whether a paper reports NEP, NDE or energy accuracy changes which appliances look good; and per-appliance averages weight a lamp and a kettle equally while energy accuracy is dominated by the kettle. Always state the metric definition alongside a number.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: From pairwise links to entities: clustering
md: Blocking decides which pairs are compared, scoring decides which pairs are linked, and clustering decides which records share an ID. Tune the threshold on labeled data, because it trades false merges against missed merges.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
md: An event loop scales because idle connections cost only a kernel watch and a small struct, and readiness is pushed to a ready list instead of scanned. It stays fast only if every callback is short: push disk I/O, DNS and CPU-heavy work to a pool, and split long jobs into chunks.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
md: A public benchmark score for a model trained on web-scale data is an upper bound on its skill on your queries, not an estimate. Before trusting a gain, ask whether the model, the synthetic training data or the judge could have seen these queries.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device
md: The defining property is not cryptography. It is that **the data stays put and only parameters move**. In the standard description of the setting, a central orchestration server organizes the training but never sees raw data.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph
md: Predicate subgraph traversal is the right search strategy (no distance computations wasted on failing nodes), but on a normal HNSW graph the predicate subgraph is sparse and disconnected. ACORN changes how the graph is built, or how neighbors are looked up, so that the predicate subgraph stays connected for any predicate.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Putting it together: routing in DeepSeek-V3
md: Batch-level balance has two weak spots the report names: imbalance inside a single sequence or small batch, and **domain shift** at inference (a deployment flooded with one kind of input overloads that domain's experts). V3 answers the first with large training batches plus the tiny sequence-wise loss, and the second with redundant experts at serving time.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Load-balanced scheduling, plan and run, and CUDA graphs
md: The docs state that `plan()` cannot be used inside a CUDA graph or `torch.compile`. With `use_cuda_graph=True` the wrapper uses caller-provided index buffers and the batch size must stay fixed for its lifetime, so engines capture one graph per batch-size bucket. For bitwise batch-invariant decode output, the docs point to `fixed_split_size` or `disable_split_kv`.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLC: breadth-first search over every reachable state
md: Liveness is only checked if you ask. In the AWS table, a lock-free data structure spec "improved confidence" but missed a liveness bug because liveness was not checked. Also remember the bounded model: no error at N = 3 says nothing about N = 4.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Microscaling: one power-of-two scale per 32 values
md: MX formats move fine-grained scaling into hardware: 32 elements share one power-of-two E8M0 scale, applied by the tensor core during the dot product. For 8-bit elements that works well. For 4-bit elements the power-of-two restriction can waste up to a whole binade of FP4's tiny 3.58-binade range.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Why exact matching fails and what an edit distance counts
md: A distance counts edits (lower is closer). A similarity is a normalized score (higher is closer). The same raw distance means very different things for short and long strings, so either normalize or make the allowed number of edits depend on length.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
md: Geometric hashing moves the expensive work offline: every model is stored under every basis. At query time one correct scene basis is enough, and it never needs to know in advance which model point it corresponds to.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Geohash: interleave the bits, name the cell
md: A shared geohash prefix guarantees closeness: both points are inside the same cell. The reverse is false: two points can be meters apart and share no prefix, because they straddle a cell boundary. Every correct proximity search must look at neighboring cells, not just one prefix.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: A caching allocator turns slow, synchronizing driver calls into fast CPU-side bookkeeping. The price is that freed memory is *kept*, so reserved memory, not allocated memory, is what other processes on the GPU see.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
md: All of these allocators are the same pattern at different layers: grab big memory rarely, carve it with your own rules, and choose block sizes that match the workload. Equal sizes kill external fragmentation; growable virtual ranges kill slivers; stream order makes reuse cheap.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: These measurements come from older GPUs (Fermi and Kepler in the post, Volta in the guide). Absolute numbers on a current GPU will differ, and larger caches can hide some waste. The sector and bank rules they illustrate are the ones the current CUDA guides still document.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
md: Rank by gap times time share, with an attainable target instead of 100 percent. The biggest gap and the biggest win are usually different kernels, and a gap on a kernel with a small time share is never worth a rewrite.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
md: GraphRAG is not a better retriever for every question. For a specific fact ("Who supplies Rover X2 motors?") plain vector RAG already finds c2, and the paper itself shows vector RAG gives the most *direct* answers. GraphRAG's measured gains are on broad sensemaking questions.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Failure modes to watch in any LLM-built graph: missed entities in large chunks, duplicate nodes from name variants, hallucinated relationships stated with confidence, and summaries that drop the specific quotes users need. Every later stage inherits these errors, and global answers rarely show the raw evidence.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Failure modes and fixes: dead groups, entropy collapse, length bias
md: RLVR mostly sharpens, it does not obviously expand. DeepSeekMath found RL raised Maj@K but not Pass@K. Yue et al. (2025) found RLVR models beat their base models at pass@1 but the base models score higher pass@k at large k: the RL model samples its best answers more reliably rather than solving problems the base model never could.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: Why a flame graph shows where time goes but not why
md: Time profiles answer *where*. Counters answer *why*: low IPC plus many cache misses points at memory, many branch misses points at prediction, high IPC with lots of instructions points at doing too much work.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: The synchronous stall is the classic THP latency spike. `/proc/vmstat` counts it: `compact_stall` increments every time a process stalls to run compaction, with `compact_success` and `compact_fail` alongside. A rising `compact_stall` next to tail-latency spikes is a strong hint.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
md: Known weak spots from the NVIDIA study: the 16K and 32K hybrids trailed the Transformer by about 1 point on long-context tasks, mostly multi-document QA where distractor passages may confuse the SSM state. Hybrids were also more prompt-sensitive: on Musique the hybrid ranged 10.63 to 16.16 across prompt tweaks vs 15.25 to 17.68 for the Transformer.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
md: Use HyDE where its strength is real: no labels, a weak or unsupervised encoder, domain or format shift, and a latency budget of seconds. Keep the query in the average, cap passage length, sample in parallel, and route by query type. The paper itself suggests serving HyDE early, then shifting traffic to a supervised retriever as logs grow, keeping HyDE for rare and emerging queries.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Why epoll plus read still costs a syscall per I/O
md: epoll is a **readiness** API: it tells you when an operation *could* succeed, then you do it. io_uring is a **completion** API: you describe the operation (read these bytes into this buffer), and the kernel tells you when it is *done* and what it returned.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: jemalloc: arenas, tcache, bitmap slabs and decay purging
md: Without `background_thread`, purging runs inside your application threads as they call into jemalloc, which adds to their tail latency, and an inactive application delays purging. jemalloc's tuning guide suggests `background_thread:true` where extra jemalloc-managed threads are acceptable.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: The nemesis: partitions, pauses, clocks and crashes
md: A distributed lock alone cannot guarantee mutual exclusion: a holder can be paused or delayed past its lease. The etcd report recommends fencing: pass a monotonically increasing token (such as the lock key's revision) with every protected operation, and have the protected resource reject tokens older than the newest it has seen.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
md: Three defences, in order: prune what cannot run, search within a budget you chose from a convergence curve, and promote only wins that are larger than the noise. A tuner without the third one is a random walk through your performance history.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: For memory-bound kernels, runtime is roughly bytes moved / bandwidth. Elementwise ops do so little math per byte that the only lever that matters is how many bytes cross the HBM boundary. Fusion cuts bytes, not FLOPs.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
md: Classic bugs: (1) forgetting the T squared factor, so changing T quietly reweights the losses; (2) using `reduction="mean"` in `kl_div`, which divides by batch size times number of classes, not batch size (the [PyTorch docs](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.KLDivLoss.html) warn about this); (3) swapping the arguments; (4) letting gradients flow into the teacher or leaving it in training mode.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
md: GQA does not reduce attention FLOPs per query head: each query head still scores every cached token. It reduces the bytes stored and read, which is what decode is bound by.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
md: Smaller caches only become speed if the attention kernel reads the compressed form directly. Dequantizing to BF16 in a separate pass gives back most of the memory traffic saved.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
md: Choose eviction by reuse pattern, not habit. LRU is a fine default; workloads with known future reuse (queued multi-turn sessions, scheduled agent steps) do much better with placement driven by the scheduler.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
md: ColBERT is not a cross-encoder with a trick. Query tokens never attend to document tokens inside the transformer. All query-document interaction happens in MaxSim, which has no trainable parameters. That is exactly why document vectors can be stored in advance.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
md: Coconut's one change: in latent mode, the next input embedding is the previous position's last hidden state instead of the embedding of a sampled token.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
md: A learned range index is a model of the key CDF plus two stored numbers per model, min_err and max_err. The model makes a guess; the error bounds turn the guess into a guarantee for every stored key.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
md: Treat the headline speedups as conditional. They were measured on in-memory, read-only, sorted integer keys. String keys (only up to 1.12 times faster in the same paper), heavy insert traffic, adversarial key sets and distribution shift all erode the gains, and a well-tuned traditional baseline matters: the SOSD benchmark was built to answer skepticism about comparisons against strong implementations.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaRank: weight each pair by what a swap does to NDCG
md: A lambda is a RankNet pair gradient scaled by how much the metric would change if the pair swapped. Pairs that cannot change the top of the list get almost no weight.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The delta rule: overwrite instead of add
md: Forgetting to normalize keys is a real bug, not a detail. Take $k_C$ scaled to length 2 and $\beta=1$: the eigenvalue is $1-4=-3$, so a component along that key is multiplied by -3, 9, -27, 81, -243 over five repeated writes.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time
md: The scheduler decides **what** runs each step, the KV cache manager decides whether it **fits**, and the executor just runs a forward pass over token ids and block tables. Almost every serving optimization in this course is a change to the first two.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Admission control is a bet about future output lengths. Reserve the worst case and you never preempt but waste memory; allocate on demand and you fit far more requests but need a preemption policy (latest arrival first, all of its blocks) and a recovery method (swap or recompute).

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Why hard constraints need filters, not similarity
md: The LLM never touches the documents. It only translates the query into a filter object. Exact enforcement is done by the search engine, which is cheap, deterministic and testable.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
md: Calls set the latency floor and the per-call overhead; tokens set the bill. Listwise minimizes calls, not tokens. PRP buys robustness to prompt order with 20 to 100 times more prompts than pointwise (220 to 1,100 times more than listwise) at k = 100.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
md: Both pointwise methods need token log-probabilities. Many chat APIs only return generated text, which is why the RankGPT authors could not run them on GPT-4. And because each passage is scored alone, the score must be comparable across passages (calibrated), which the PRP paper argues LLMs are not trained to provide.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
md: Judge a match by how much better it is than the runner-up, not by its absolute distance. The ratio d1/d2 adapts to how distinctive each descriptor is.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The ABA problem: when a matching CAS is still wrong
md: CAS compares bits, not history. Any lock-free algorithm that frees or reuses nodes must either version its pointers or guarantee that no thread can still hold a reference to a node that gets reused.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
md: Parsing accuracy is not the goal; downstream behaviour is. SHISO parsed 93 percent of messages into the right groups and still produced 7 times the false alarms, because the templates it got wrong were ones the detector was sensitive to. Always evaluate a parser change by re-running the task that consumes its output.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: With dynamic scaling the RoPE of every cached token changes when $s$ changes. The YaRN paper notes the correct implementation caches keys *before* applying RoPE; caching rotated keys silently mixes two different scalings.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
md: A looped transformer decouples depth from parameter count. $(k \otimes L)$ has $k$ layers of parameters and $kL$ layers of sequential computation.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Approximate unlearning: gradient ascent, collapse and NPO
md: "Loss on the forget set went up" is not evidence of good unlearning. GA can drive that loss arbitrarily high by wrecking the model. Always read forget metrics next to utility metrics and next to the retrained reference.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Truncate, then re-normalize: the mechanics on a toy vector
md: Re-normalizing the query alone never changes a ranking: it scales every score by the same number. What changes rankings is the documents' prefix lengths, so re-normalize the stored document prefixes (or compute true cosine). OpenAI's embedding guide says the same: if you shorten vectors yourself, normalize them.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP
md: The 5as/h term assumes attention materializes the s x s score matrix. Fused attention kernels (FlashAttention style, as in Transformer Engine) never store it, so most of that term disappears by itself. Megatron Core's config even warns that with fused attention there is no need to put core_attn in --recompute-modules.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Why freed memory does not go back: pages, arenas, purging
md: Setting `dirty_decay_ms` to 0 is not a free fix. The manual says it purges dirty pages immediately when they are created, so every page that empties pays for a purge, and every later reuse pays a page fault. It lowers RSS that is merely waiting; it does nothing for pages pinned by live objects.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: `volatile` is not an ordering. In standard C++, volatile accesses are not atomic and do not order other memory, so they cannot be used for synchronization between threads. (MSVC gives volatile acquire/release semantics by default on x86 targets; that is a compiler extension, not the language.)

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Do not benchmark a reclamation scheme with one thread on an idle machine. The cost differences that matter, garbage growth under preemption and fence cost on long traversals, only appear with oversubscribed threads, update-heavy workloads and long data structures.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: ArcFace: putting an angular margin inside a classifier
md: The class weights only cover training identities. At test time you discard them and compare normalized features with cosine similarity, exactly as with a triplet-trained model. A large classification accuracy on training classes is not the goal.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
md: Misconception: "disabling ASLR and pinning the CPU makes my benchmark correct". They reduce run-to-run noise, which narrows intervals. A narrow interval around a biased setup is a confidently wrong answer.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
md: The Miles fault-tolerance page is marked **outdated**: it describes the pre-refactor stack, and new machinery is still being merged. Also note that P2P writes are bounded by `--p2p-transfer-timeout` (default 30 s) and a failed write fails the update; the docs state there is no automatic retry or fallback to broadcast.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
md: Reported speedups are relative to specific baselines on specific traces: B-LRU on six CDN traces, a tuned weighted fair scheduler on TPC-H mixes, a read-optimized B-tree on read-only integer keys. A different workload, or a stronger baseline, can shrink the gain to zero.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Why one phrasing of a question misses relevant documents
md: Retrieval quality depends on the exact words of the query. Multi-query retrieval treats the user's wording as one sample from many possible phrasings and retrieves with several samples instead of betting on one.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes
md: Precompute versus interact. The more of the query-document comparison happens at query time, the more accurate and the more expensive the scorer. Bi-encoders and late interaction can serve as first stages over an index; cross-encoders only fit on short candidate lists.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
md: MTP gives two separate benefits: a training signal that can make the main model better, and heads that can draft tokens for exact, faster greedy decoding. You can use the first without the second by discarding the heads.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Scaling Muon to LLMs, distributing it, and choosing an optimizer
md: Do not judge an optimizer by a single untuned comparison. The Muon post argues that most papers claiming to beat AdamW used undertuned baselines, and proposes competitive benchmarks (like the NanoGPT speedrun record, where anyone can revert to AdamW) as the standard of evidence.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: A lock is two things at once: mutual exclusion (one atomic read-modify-write decides a single winner) and visibility (Acquire on lock, Release on unlock, so each unlock happens-before the next lock).

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC is not the same as no locking. Two transactions that update the *same* row still conflict: the second one waits for the first to commit or roll back. MVCC only stops readers and writers from blocking each other.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI = snapshot isolation plus non-blocking tracking of rw edges. It aborts a transaction in any dangerous structure, so every committed set is serializable; the application's job is to retry on 40001.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints
md: Theoretical FLOP savings are not speedups. A sparse attention method is only fast if the GPU reads fewer bytes in contiguous chunks during every phase (training, prefill, decode), and it only keeps quality if the model is trained with the sparsity.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Global hashes, PDQ included, do poorly when one image is a **crop** of another; the PDQ document lists deep crops as out of scope. ImageHash's documentation shows how fast aHash degrades with rotation on its test image: 2 bits at 1 degree, 11 at 6 degrees, 21 at 26 degrees. Large borders, overlaid text and memes also defeat them.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
md: NUMA means the cost of a cache miss depends on which node holds the page. Keep each thread's data on the node where the thread runs.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
md: Locality needs both halves: pages on the right node, and threads that stay there. Pin, or let NUMA balancing migrate pages, and verify placement with numa_maps rather than allocation counters.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
md: Raising the confidence threshold does not always raise precision. It only helps if the boxes it removes are mostly false positives. A confidently wrong box, like B3 at 0.75, survives every threshold that keeps it.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
md: Write data under fresh names, then commit a reference atomically. Use a create-if-absent or compare-and-swap on the commit point so that exactly one writer can ever extend the history.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Traces: spans, context propagation, and what sampling throws away
md: A trace is kept or dropped as a whole, and the decision is made by whoever starts it. Head sampling trades away rare events; tail sampling buys them back with buffering and stateful collectors. Never read a trace count as a request count.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
md: Forgetting to normalize is a classic bug. Raw pixel coordinates from a 1700 x 2200 scan exceed the 1024-entry position tables and crash with an index error, or, if clipped, silently collapse the lower part of the page onto the same embedding.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Declare every real dependency on the target that uses it, with the narrowest correct scope: PRIVATE if only the .cpp files use it, PUBLIC if your headers expose it, INTERFACE if only your headers do. CMake then derives include paths, definitions and link order for you.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Do not add `@pytest.mark.flaky` or `xfail` to a test your PR broke. Maintainers read that as hiding a failure. If you believe a failure is pre-existing flakiness, show evidence: the same test failing on `main` or on other PRs, or a seed that reproduces it without your change.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: You may not add a Reviewed-by, Tested-by or Acked-by tag for someone just because they said nice things. The kernel guide says these need the named person's explicit permission; only Cc:, Reported-by: and Suggested-by: can be added with implicit permission.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Before using an AI tool on a contribution, find the project's policy (CONTRIBUTING, developer docs, or the docs on patch submission). Then: never submit what you cannot explain, disclose as the project asks, and never let a tool add your sign-off.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: `--force-with-lease` says "overwrite only if the remote is still what I last fetched". Add `--force-if-includes` so a fetch alone does not count as having seen the remote's commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: The most common CLA failure is an email mismatch: the commits use a personal or unregistered address while the agreement (or the employer's group) lists another. Fix the author email and rewrite the commits, not the agreement.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values
md: Significant is not the same as large. benchstat's docs stress that with enough low-noise data even very small changes become significant. Report the size of the change and its spread, and use the test only to answer "is this more than noise?"

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A bug report's first job is to let the maintainer make the failure happen themselves. Everything else in the report (description, guesses about the cause) comes second.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: A flaky repro is not done until it fails every time or you know its failure rate. Pin seeds and inputs, report versions, and repeat runs enough times that a PASS means something.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Self-review first, then mark ready. A reviewable PR is focused, explained, clean, and honestly labeled as draft or ready.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Longest-prefix-first can starve a request whose prefix is never cached, since others keep jumping ahead. The SGLang paper says so and leaves fair scheduling as future work.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols
md: Missing callers, a detached tower over [unknown], or hex instead of names are not hot spots. They are profiler blind spots. Fix frame pointers or symbols before you trust the picture.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Alignment: which addresses a type is allowed to start at
md: "x86 handles misaligned loads, so alignment does not matter" is a common misconception. In C the rule is in the language, not just the CPU: converting a pointer to a type whose alignment the address does not satisfy is **undefined behavior** (C11 6.3.2.3p7). The optimizer may assume every `int *` is 4-aligned, whatever the CPU tolerates.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Scoring poses with Object Keypoint Similarity
md: OKS is averaged per object over *labeled* keypoints, so a person with only 4 labeled points counts as much as one with 17. Also, persons too small to have keypoint labels are not evaluated, and at most 20 detections per image are scored. Comparing OKS numbers across datasets with different skeletons or sigmas is meaningless.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Query planners: choosing a strategy by selectivity
md: No single plan wins everywhere. Broad filters favor graph search with the filter applied during or after it; restrictive filters favor brute force over an allow list; the middle is where graphs fragment and filter-aware indexes like ACORN and Filtered-DiskANN earn their keep. The deciding input is the estimated number of matches.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
md: An ORM gets one label per solution and must discover where errors are. A PRM is told where the first error is. That extra information is why PRMs rank solutions better on hard problems, and why they can reject right answers reached by wrong reasoning.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a context switch, step by step
md: Register save and restore is the same for every switch. The difference between a thread switch and a process switch is the address space: if `next` shares `prev`'s memory, the page table stays loaded and the TLB stays valid.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Twenty letters, one backbone: the design problem
md:
Two separate objects, and you must keep them apart:

- **sequence**: which of the 20 amino acids sits at each position (discrete, one symbol per residue)
- **backbone**: where the N, CA, C and O atoms of every residue sit in 3D space (continuous coordinates)

The chain folds into one preferred backbone shape, and that shape is what gives the protein its function.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
md: Create the synonym set before the index that references it. Elastic's guide warns that an index pointing at a missing set becomes inoperable and must be deleted and re-created, or closed and re-opened.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Plain binary quantization: one sign bit per dimension
md: Binary quantization = sign of each coordinate, compared with XOR and popcount. It buys 32x memory and very cheap comparisons, but the distance it produces is coarse and has no error guarantee.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
md: Stored on a majority is not the same as committed. An entry from an *earlier* term can sit on a majority and still be erased by a later leader. Commitment is only decided by counting replicas of an entry from the leader's *current* term, which then commits everything before it.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Evaluating retrieval and generation separately
md: LLM judges are themselves models. On the WikiEval dataset, Ragas agreed with human annotators 95% of the time on faithfulness, 78% on answer relevance and 70% on context relevance. Spot-check the judge on your data, and note that context precision as computed here treats a 44-word chunk and a 12-word chunk the same, so it does not see how much noise a big chunk brings.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: Every cutoff metric hides a choice: the cutoff, the relevance threshold (grade at least 1 here), the divisor, and what to do with short runs. Two papers both reporting "MAP@10" may be computing different numbers.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
md: Polling the trailer only works if the NIC writes the message in increasing address order. FaRM notes that many NICs, including theirs, guarantee this for RDMA writes but not reads. It is a hardware property, not a verbs promise: registering memory with `IBV_ACCESS_RELAXED_ORDERING` explicitly gives up write-after-write ordering.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
md: Interpolation is not prediction. It never invents a position: it only blends two snapshots the server really sent. The cost is that every remote entity is shown late by the buffer delay, which is why aiming needs lag compensation.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
md: Retrieval must be cheap per item (dot products over precomputed vectors); ranking can be expensive per item. In-batch negatives are sampled by popularity, so correct each logit by log p_j.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: A query plan is a tree of operators that pull rows
md: Cost units are not milliseconds. They are relative estimates the planner uses to compare plans. To see real time, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually runs the query.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
md: A commit is only as safe as the set of machines that had it when the client was told "ok". Every replication knob is a choice of *how many* and *which* machines that set must include, paid for in commit latency.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: KL regularization: a leash, not a cure
md: KL regularization and early stopping limit the *amount* of optimization, which keeps you on the rising side of the Goodhart curve. They cannot tell a good high-reward behavior from a bad one. Only a better reward, a conservative reward, or an outside check can do that.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
md: Sync cost = bytes / bandwidth + resharding. The bytes are fixed by model size and precision; good systems avoid gathering the full model anywhere, send each rank only its shard, and keep the transfer off the critical path.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Walking the dependency graph to the anomalous frontier
md: Correlation is not causation, and the SRE troubleshooting chapter names the two ways this bites. First, correlated events often share a cause: packet loss in a cluster and failed disks in the same cluster correlate because a power event hit both, not because either caused the other. Second, as you monitor more metrics it becomes inevitable that some will correlate well with your symptom purely by coincidence.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Ties, missing documents and the window size
md: Pagination: in Elasticsearch, if `from + size` exceeds `rank_window_size` you get 0 results, and pages are only consistent while `rank_window_size` stays fixed. Changing W re-ranks everything, as the animation shows, so never vary it between page requests.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
md: Direction matters at the boundary: Rust calling C uses `to_result`/`from_err_ptr`; C calling Rust uses a trampoline that returns `err.to_errno()`. Ownership crossing the boundary goes through `into_foreign` once and `from_foreign` once.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Worked example: weighted vtime fairness in a few lines of BPF
md: scx_simple charges `SCX_SLICE_DFL - p->scx.slice`. Its own comment warns that a task that yields has its slice zeroed and so is charged a full slice. Precise schedulers take explicit timestamps in `running` and `stopping` instead.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Playing against your past self: SPIN and Self-Rewarding LMs
md: Rising numbers are not proof that quality rose. Average response length on AlpacaEval grew from 1092 (M1) to 1552 (M2) to 2552 (M3), and length is known to correlate with judged quality. The authors list reward hacking within the framework as an open question, and note that LLMs supply both the training reward and (through GPT-4) the evaluation, which needs deeper analysis.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Scaling out: TP, DP, DP attention, EP and cache-aware routing
md: Cache locality and load balance pull against each other. Sending every request of a hot prefix to one worker maximizes hits and can overload that worker; the balance thresholds exist to break locality when queues diverge. The gateway's trees are approximate: they are inferred from routed text, not read from the workers, so they can be stale.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Real engines: turn costs, live traffic and time-dependent travel
md: No technique wins on every axis. Look at query time, preprocessing time, memory, how quickly new traffic weights can be applied, and whether turns and other metrics are supported. A static fastest-route server and a live-traffic service often choose differently.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
md: Every hand-written SIMD loop has a vector body, a horizontal reduction and a tail. A vector reduction adds in a different order than the scalar loop, so float results can change, which is why compilers need permission to reassociate.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: Bump allocation: a bounds check and a pointer add
md: "Arena" means different things in different allocators. In this lesson it is a bump region freed all at once. In jemalloc (and glibc malloc) an *arena* is an independent general-purpose heap with its own locks, used so threads contend less; you still free objects one by one there.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Placing training and rollout: colocated or separate GPUs
md: "Disaggregated" here is about trainer versus rollout GPUs. It is unrelated to PD disaggregation (`--prefill-num-servers`), which splits SGLang's own prefill and decode work, and it does not imply async training by itself.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
md: Words to keep apart: a **latent** is a unit of the SAE; a **feature** is the concept you hope it captures. Gemma Scope says 'latents' for exactly this reason. A latent with a clean name is a hypothesis about a model feature, not proof of one.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Six sensors and a blank map: interpolation as weighted averaging
md: Interpolation is not the same as smoothing. Most of these methods are *exact*: the surface passes through every reading. That is right for precise instruments and wrong for noisy cheap sensors, where you want a method that can treat part of each reading as measurement error.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Which map to trust: leave-one-out cross-validation
md: Choose interpolators by held-out error, not by reputation. Leave-one-out RMSE (or blocked cross-validation) compares methods on your data, and the standardized errors tell you whether kriging's uncertainty can be trusted.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: From 16,000 samples a second to a log-mel spectrogram
md: A log-mel spectrogram is 80 numbers every 10 ms. Whisper's 30 second input is therefore an 80 x 3000 matrix: the model never sees raw samples.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: Stack memory lives exactly as long as the function call that created it. Allocation and release are a pointer adjustment, which is why the size must be bounded and why anything that must outlive the call has to go somewhere else: the heap.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
md: Most page faults are normal: they are how Linux allocates memory on first touch and copies pages only on write. Count them with getrusage or `perf`; worry about major faults and fault storms, not their existence.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Ingest: MQTT at the edge, a Kafka log in the middle
md: Kafka turns backpressure from data loss into delay: as long as retention covers the backlog, a slow consumer only falls behind. The bounded buffers inside the processor are what make the slowdown propagate instead of growing memory without bound.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Scaled dot-product attention, computed on four tokens
md: Scaling by the square root of d_k is not mainly about float overflow (implementations subtract the row max before exponentiating anyway). It keeps softmax out of its saturated, near one-hot region so gradients stay usable as d_k grows.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
md: Saturation does not mean repeated terms are ignored. With k1 = 1.2, going from 1 to 2 occurrences still raises the factor from 0.45 to 0.62. It means each extra occurrence is worth less than the one before, with a hard ceiling.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
md: Pre-LN vs post-LN is not cosmetic. Xiong et al. show that in the original post-LN Transformer the gradients near the output are large at initialization, which is why it needs a careful learning-rate warmup. Placing LayerNorm inside the residual branch, as GPT-2 does, gives well-behaved gradients at initialization.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Derivative rules and the chain rule for nested functions
md: A common slip is evaluating the outer derivative at $x$ instead of at the inner value. Here $f'(u) = 2u$ must use $u = 7$, giving 14, not $2 \times 2 = 4$. That is why the forward values are computed and stored first: the backward step needs them.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Expansion and quoting: why rm $f can delete the wrong files
md: Do not test your quoting in zsh and assume bash agrees. zsh, the default interactive shell on macOS, does **not** word-split unquoted parameter expansions unless the `SH_WORD_SPLIT` option is set. Scripts that start with `#!/bin/bash` or `#!/bin/sh` follow the splitting rules shown here.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Learning word vectors by predicting their neighbours
md: Skip-gram is not trained to be a good language model; the prediction task is a pretext. Mikolov et al. say plainly that the skip-gram model is only concerned with learning high-quality vector representations. After training, the output layer is usually thrown away and the input vectors are kept as the embeddings.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
md: Doubling peak TFLOP/s does almost nothing for batch-1 decode. What helps is moving fewer bytes per token (smaller or quantized weights, which for example halve the bytes at 8 bits) or using each byte for more tokens (batching, next lessons).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The CPU loop: fetch, decode, execute, repeat
md: Simplified: real CPUs pipeline and overlap many instructions, and even execute them out of order. But they are built so that the visible result is exactly as if each instruction ran one at a time in program order, which is why this model is the right one to reason with.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Pretraining: next-token loss over trillions of tokens
md: A low pretraining loss does not mean a helpful model. The loss rewards matching the *distribution* of internet text, including its errors, rudeness and rambling. That is exactly why the later stages exist.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: From grep to the inverted index
md: An inverted index alone does not rank anything. Boolean retrieval returns an unordered set: a document either matches or it does not. Ranking needs term weights, which lessons 4 and 5 add on top of the same postings.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Inverted indexes in real engines: compression, updates, Lucene
md: TF-IDF still has two flaws that cosine only partly fixes: tf keeps growing with every repetition (keyword stuffing pays), and length normalization is crude. BM25, the next course, keeps the same inverted index and replaces the weighting with a saturating tf and a tunable length normalization.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Object lifetimes: automatic, static and malloc'd memory
md: Before you keep a pointer, ask how long the object behind it lives. Locals die when their function returns, malloc'd memory dies at free, and realloc can retire the old address at any call.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
md: The rule is not "only one reference to a variable per function". Sequential borrows are fine, as are many shared ones. The error only appears when a `&mut` borrow overlaps any other live borrow of the same value.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A matrix is a function that moves every vector
md: Not every useful function is linear. $f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \ne 0$ is **affine**: it moves the origin, so $f(\mathbf{0}) = \mathbf{b}$ instead of $\mathbf{0}$. Neural network layers are affine, and their activation functions (like ReLU) are not linear at all. That nonlinearity is what lets a deep network do more than one big matrix could.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: stepping downhill, and how big a step
md: Gradient descent: $w \leftarrow w - \eta \nabla L$. On a quadratic, each step multiplies the error by $1 - \eta\lambda$ per direction, so it converges only if $\eta < 2/\lambda$ for every curvature $\lambda$, and the sharpest direction sets the limit.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies
md: Keep the cached values. The forward pass is not just for the prediction: the backward pass will reuse every $z^l$ and $a^l$ computed here, so frameworks store them.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
md: Any read-modify-write of shared data (even `x++`) is several instructions, and a context switch can split them. Protect every critical section with a lock, and build locks on atomic hardware instructions, never on plain loads and stores.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
md: Linearity of expectation needs no independence, but the variance addition rule does. For dependent variables, $\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$, where the **covariance** measures how they move together.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: $C \approx 6ND$. For a fixed budget, parameters and tokens trade off one for one in ratio: double $N$ and you must halve $D$.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
md: A common bug: dividing by the number of relevant documents *retrieved* (4) instead of all relevant documents (5). That gives 0.642 instead of 0.513 and silently rewards systems that retrieve fewer relevant documents.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Training embeddings with in-batch negatives
md: In-batch negatives assume the other passages are wrong. If the batch holds two copies of the same passage, or two paraphrased questions, the loss pushes a correct answer away. sentence-transformers recommends the `NO_DUPLICATES` batch sampler for this reason. Hard negatives mined automatically can also be unlabeled positives, so they need filtering.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
md: Encoding is **not** "find the longest matching token from the left" and not "pick the segmentation with fewest tokens". BPE applies merges greedily in the order they were learned. A different procedure over the same vocabulary can give a different split, and the model was trained on BPE's split.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: A debugging recipe: loss at init, overfit one batch, read the curves
md: Every check has a **known right answer**: loss at init equals $\ln C$, one batch overfits to about zero, the real model beats an input-independent baseline. Add one piece of complexity at a time and re-check, so when something breaks you know which change did it.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Why resampling your own outputs erases rare events
md: Model collapse is not caused by a bad model or a bug. In this example fitting is exact. The finite sample alone, which Shumailov et al. call **statistical approximation error**, is enough to drive the process.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: vdso(7) states that calls served by the vDSO do not appear in `strace` output and are invisible to seccomp filters. A trace with zero `clock_gettime` lines does not mean the program never asks for the time.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Coordinated omission: the load tester stops looking when it hurts
md: Coordinated omission does not make individual samples wrong: the 2 ms readings were real. The bug is which samples exist. The tester samples less often precisely when the server is slow, so the sample set is biased toward good moments. No statistic computed afterwards can recover samples that were never taken.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
md: Every time-scoped question becomes interval arithmetic once two things are fixed: the reference date, and the convention for partial dates. Allen relations, current-role tests and window clipping are all a few endpoint comparisons.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: The best use of test-time compute depends on the prompt. Search is most valuable where the model is weak but not hopeless; on easy prompts it can hurt by exploiting the verifier.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
md: Titans' memory update = gradient descent with momentum (carry surprise forward) and weight decay (forget), all gated per token. Momentum keeps writing after a surprising event; forgetting keeps a fixed-size memory from overflowing.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers
md: Tiering wins only if the *hot* pages live in the fast tier. The capacity of each tier matters less than the fraction of accesses it serves. Everything in this course is machinery for keeping $h$ high cheaply.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Naive, seasonal naive and simple exponential smoothing
md: A parameter fitted to minimize one-step in-sample error is not automatically good at the horizon you care about. Always evaluate at the real horizon on data the fit never saw.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
md: Autotuning has costs you do not see in steady state: the first call for each new `key` value compiles and benchmarks every config, and each distinct constexpr combination is a separate compiled kernel. Keep `key` to arguments that really change the best config, and use `prune_configs_by` to drop hopeless candidates.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
md: No axis is free. Discrete plus causal is the simplest to train and serve; continuous plus bidirectional plus separate encoders has led the reported GenEval numbers in these papers, at the cost of more moving parts. Pick based on what the product must do well, then evaluate both sides of the model.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Why one vector distance is mostly a memory problem
md: At hundreds of dimensions, a distance does about 0.5 to 0.75 FLOPs per byte of vector it reads. SIMD makes the arithmetic cheap; after that, the bytes you move (and the cache misses you take) decide the speed.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
md: Turning on mmap does not shrink an index; it only lets the OS evict parts of it. If the hot working set does not fit, latency can fall off a cliff, because each miss is a disk read instead of a DRAM access.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and running verl in practice
md: verl in one sentence: a single Python controller expresses the RL algorithm as calls on WorkerGroups; each WorkerGroup runs a training or inference engine SPMD on a resource pool; DataProto carries the batch between them; and actor and rollout share GPUs by resharding or sleeping instead of keeping two copies.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
md: FVD alone cannot tell whether a model listens to actions. A model that ignores the controls but produces realistic clips can score well. That is why Genie pairs FVD with delta PSNR, and why its pixel-input LAM was chosen despite a slightly worse Platformers FVD (40.1 vs 38.8): its controllability was much higher (1.91 vs 1.33).

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
md: Kumar et al. note fine-tuning can still beat linear probing out of distribution when the pretrained features are weak or the shift is small (CIFAR-10 to CIFAR-10.1). LP-FT is a strong default, not a law.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Codebook collapse: measuring and fixing unused codes
md: Bigger codebooks do not automatically mean more capacity. FSQ (Mentzer et al., 2023) found that VQ's reconstruction FID was best at about 2^11 codes and then stopped improving, at the same point where VQ's codebook usage began to drop, despite an entropy regulariser.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: KV cache layout and block sizes per backend
md: A KV cache layout is chosen once for the whole model, not per layer. If two backends in one model share no layout, startup fails with *No KV cache layout satisfies every supported set* rather than converting at runtime.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Reading a receipt into validated JSON
md: Validate meaning, not just shape. Documents carry their own checksums: line items sum to a subtotal, subtotal plus tax equals the total, dates fall in a plausible range. Use them.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
md: Universal does not mean practical. Every cell carries a full object state, and every operation contends on the single end of one log, so operations on different parts of the object (a queue's head and tail) still conflict. Kogan and Petrank point to these two costs, state copying and no disjoint-access parallelism, as why universal constructions are hardly considered practical.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: Every global score is an area-weighted average. Weights proportional to cos(latitude) count each unit of Earth's surface once.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front
md: Cosine couples the **shape** of the LR curve to the **end date** of training. You must choose the training length before you start, and every checkpoint before the end is half-annealed.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: splice and tee: pipes as buffers of page references
md: Pipes are the kernel's zero-copy buffer: slots of reference-counted page pointers. splice moves those pointers between a pipe and any descriptor, tee duplicates them, and sendfile itself runs on this machinery with a hidden internal pipe.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
md: Constrain the LLM to the label set, read a probability per label, and divide by the probabilities a content-free input gets under the same prompt. Calibration fixes a constant shift; it cannot fix a model that does not understand the labels.
